summary: Describes using DTLS over SCTP, giving privacy for SCTP applications and letting client-server applications communicate in a way designed to prevent eavesdropping and detect tampering.

eli5.summary: SCTP carries messages between computers. This wraps them in a secret code so no one can read or change them in transit.

questions: why not use tls over sctp
how does dtls use sctp streams
how are sctp auth keys derived from dtls
subtitle: How to protect SCTP associations with DTLS while keeping streams, unordered delivery and partial reliability.

tldr.problem: TLS over SCTP (RFC 3436) cannot do unordered delivery or partial reliability, needs the same number of streams in both directions, and uses a TLS connection per bidirectional stream.
tldr.mechanism: Run DTLS inside a single SCTP association, with each SCTP user message holding exactly one DTLS record, DTLS's own retransmission, replay detection and Path MTU discovery switched off, and SCTP-AUTH keys derived from the DTLS master secret.
tldr.outcome: Applications get privacy and tamper detection while using almost all SCTP transport features, with a user message limit of 2^14 bytes.

today: RFC 6083 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8996. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why DTLS Over SCTP
sections.content:
TLS is designed to run on a reliable, in-sequence byte stream such as TCP. RFC 3436 put TLS on top of SCTP, but with serious limits: no unordered delivery of user messages, no partial reliability from RFC 3758, the same number of streams in both directions, and one TLS connection for every bidirectional stream.

This document uses Datagram TLS (DTLS, RFC 4347) over SCTP (RFC 4960) instead. DTLS/SCTP preserves message boundaries, supports many unidirectional and bidirectional streams, ordered and unordered delivery, partial reliability and dynamic address reconfiguration (RFC 5061).

Two limits remain: the maximum user message size is 2^14 bytes, which is the DTLS limit, and the DTLS user cannot do SCTP-AUTH key management because the DTLS layer does it. The SCTP implementation must support fragmentation of user messages and the SCTP authentication extension (RFC 4895).
sections.eli5: The old way needed a separate locked tunnel for each lane. The new way uses one lock for the whole road, so every lane keeps working as before.

sections.title: Adapting DTLS to Run Over SCTP
sections.content:
DTLS normally copes with an unreliable network. SCTP already provides reliability, sequencing, Path MTU discovery and fragmentation, so several DTLS features are switched off:

  • Message size: the DTLS path MTU MUST be considered to be 2^14.
  • Replay detection: MUST NOT be used, because it could drop messages that SCTP delivers reliably.
  • Path MTU discovery: DTLS's own MUST NOT be used, since SCTP does this.
  • Retransmission: DTLS retransmission procedures MUST NOT be used, since SCTP provides reliable, in-sequence service where needed.

The document is based on RFC 4347 and expects the approach to work with future DTLS versions.
sections.eli5: The lock already has its own helpers for carrying and re-sending, so the delivery service's helpers do those jobs and the lock's helpers are told to stay quiet.

sections.title: Mapping Records, Streams and Chunks
sections.content:
The supported maximum SCTP user message length MUST be at least 2^14 + 2048 + 13 = 18445 bytes, covering the largest DTLSCiphertext fragment plus the 13-byte DTLS record header. Every SCTP user message MUST consist of exactly one DTLS record.

Each DTLS connection MUST be established and terminated within the same SCTP association and MUST NOT span several associations.

All ChangeCipherSpec, Alert and Handshake messages MUST go on stream 0 with unlimited reliability and ordered delivery. ApplicationData messages SHOULD use other streams, but MAY use stream 0 for everything if head of line blocking does not matter.

Applications SHOULD register and use a separate payload protocol identifier (PPID) for use over DTLS and SHOULD NOT reuse the one registered for plain SCTP. There is no specific PPID for DTLS itself.

DATA chunks MUST be sent authenticated as in RFC 4895, so an attacker cannot change the stream a message is on or its ordered or unordered flag. If PR-SCTP is used, FORWARD-TSN chunks MUST also be authenticated.
sections.eli5: Each parcel holds exactly one locked box. Lane 0 is for the lock's own setup notes, and your actual goods can travel in the other lanes.

sections.title: Handshake, Keys and Shutdown
sections.content:
DTLS discards messages from older epochs after some time, which is not acceptable for reliable transfer. So before sending a ChangeCipherSpec, all outstanding SCTP user messages MUST have been acknowledged and not be revocable by the peer. Before processing a received ChangeCipherSpec, other buffered SCTP user messages MUST be read and processed by DTLS. Messages arriving between ChangeCipherSpec and Finished in the new epoch MUST be buffered by DTLS until Finished is read.

The endpoint-pair shared secret for Shared Key Identifier 0 is empty and MUST be used when establishing a DTLS connection. Whenever the master key changes, a 64-byte shared secret is derived from each master secret with the exporter of RFC 5705, using the label EXPORTER_DTLS_OVER_SCTP and no context. The new Shared Key Identifier is the old one plus 1, and after 65535 it becomes 1. The active SCTP-AUTH key MUST be switched before sending Finished, and the old key SHOULD be removed once the peer's Finished arrives.

A CloseNotify MUST only be sent after all outstanding SCTP user messages are acknowledged and not revocable, and buffered messages MUST be processed before handling a received CloseNotify. Renegotiation is available, and it is up to the upper layer to allow it, with the caveat that it may change security parameters.
sections.eli5: When the lock is changed, everything already on the road must arrive first. The new key is worked out from the old secret, and the key number goes up by one each time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4347, RFC 4895 and RFC 4960 also apply.

DTLS endpoints can be authenticated by IP addresses in certificates, but an SCTP endpoint can use several addresses, so DTLS records may come from a different address than the one authenticated. That is fine as long as no security decisions rest on the address. The general rule is to base decisions on the peer's authenticated identity, not its transport layer identity.

The stream identifier, the ordered/unordered flag and the payload protocol identifier are not protected by DTLS. They sit in the SCTP DATA chunk header and travel as clear text. Finally, DTLS permits cipher suites with a NULL cipher, and negotiating one gives no privacy for user messages.
sections.eli5: The locked box hides what is inside, but the address label on the outside, such as the lane number, can still be read.
